# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

## 4. Claim only what you can show
End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. Installed, executed and accepted are different states, and only a person can accept. Mark anything you could not check as `[unverified]`.

## Work in progress

I've written `baseline.md` at the project root. The headline is a 6-day median, but that figure leaves out the open queries, so it understates the typical wait.

**Baseline (60 queries)**

| Category | Queries | Still open |
|---|---|---|
| Price mismatch | 17 | 7 |
| Goods not received | 16 | 3 |
| Missing purchase order | 15 | 6 |
| Duplicate invoice | 9 | 0 |
| Bank details change | 2 | 0 |
| Blank category | 1 | 0 |

- **Median time to close:** 6 calendar days, across the 42 closed queries with usable dates. Mean 9.7, range 1 to 30.
- **Still open:** 16 of 60 (27%), aged 51 to 112 days as at 31 October. Taking those at no less than their current age, the median across all 58 queries with usable dates is at least 12 days. That is a lower bound, not a measured figure.

**Don't trust yet**

- **Q-017** is closed before it was opened (close 8 July, open 11 July). I excluded it from timing.
- **Q-045** has an opened date of 2026-02-31, which isn't a real date. I excluded it from timing.
- **Q-032** has no category. It appears as "(blank)".
- **Q-058** repeats Q-012 exactly, apart from the query ID: same supplier, invoice INV-55898, site and dates. It may be a double entry. Removing it changes Duplicate invoice to 8 and leaves the median at 6.
- **Intake may have stopped.** No query was opened after 17 September, though today is 31 October. Confirm the export window before quoting volumes.
- **Open items may be stale.** Some of the 16 may have been closed in practice and never updated.
- **Days are calendar days.** I don't know whether the system counts business days.
- **The file can't answer the AI question.** It has no staff time, cost, resolution outcome or query text. So it cannot say what share an assistant could handle.

**Choices I made**

- Kept the bad rows in the category counts and excluded them from timing only.
- Reported the median on closed queries and added the open-query lower bound alongside it, rather than choosing one.

# Proposal: planned maintenance and repairs for the Northgate Cycles cargo e-bike fleet

**For:** Sam Reid, Head of Operations, Northgate Cycles
**From:** Riverside Fleet Care, [TO CONFIRM: sender name and role]
**Date:** 31 October 2026
**Decision needed by:** end of November 2026, with your finance director

## The problem, as you described it

Northgate runs 64 cargo e-bikes for last-mile grocery delivery across three hubs. On a bad week, 10 or more are waiting for parts or a mechanic. That is roughly one bike in six off the road at any time. Your in-house mechanic left in August and has not been replaced, so the in-house capacity to fix bikes went with that role.

You need two things from a supplier: a monthly cost you can predict, and a way to report fleet availability to your board every month.

## Our proposal

- **Planned maintenance for all 64 bikes at £38 per bike per month: £2,432 per month, or £29,184 over a year.** We have no minimum fleet size, so this is the price for your whole fleet.
- **Reactive repairs** when a bike breaks down, at £55 per hour plus parts, billed for the work actually done.
- **A monthly availability report** for your board, showing how many bikes are on the road, how many are off it and why. [TO CONFIRM BEFORE SENDING: report content and format, which is not yet in our approved service terms.]

## Why Riverside

**A team, not one person.** We have 11 technicians. When one person leaves, the work carries on. That is the gap Northgate has now.

**Certified on drive systems.** Every one of our technicians holds manufacturer certification for at least two drive systems. Send us the drive systems on your 64 bikes and we will confirm the cover before you decide.

**Insured.** We carry £5m public liability insurance.

**Customers stay.** 94% of customers who started with us in 2024 renewed in 2025. We have 42 business customers as at 30 September [TO CONFIRM: year]. We were founded in 2019 and are based in Bristol.

**Honest about response times.** Our average on-site response in 2025 was 1.8 working days. That is an average, not a guarantee. Before you sign, we propose to agree a written response standard for each of your three hubs, so the standard you hold us to is clear from the start.

## The money

| Item | Price | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Planned maintenance, 64 bikes | £38 per bike per month, £2,432 per month | £29,184 a year |
| Reactive repairs | £55 per hour plus parts | Billed as used. Not in the monthly price. |

**An example, not a forecast.** If 10 bikes each needed one hour of repair in a month, the labour would be £550, plus parts. This assumes one hour per bike and is there to show how reactive costs scale.

**How to check it against your own numbers.** Compare your full cost of an in-house mechanic (salary, on-costs, and cover for holiday and sickness) with the planned maintenance fee plus the reactive repairs you expect. You know those figures better than we do, so we would rather you test

# Proposal: Planned Maintenance for the Northgate Cycles Cargo E-Bike Fleet

**Prepared for:** Sam Reid, Head of Operations, Northgate Cycles
**Prepared by:** Riverside Fleet Care
**Date:** 31 October 2026

---

## 1. Summary

Northgate Cycles runs 64 cargo e-bikes across three hubs, and on a bad week ten or more of them are off the road waiting for parts or a mechanic. Since your in-house mechanic left in August, that problem has had no owner.

We propose a planned-maintenance plan for the whole fleet at **£38 per bike per month**. For 64 bikes that is:

| | Per bike | 64-bike fleet |
|---|---|---|
| Per month | £38 | **£2,432** |
| Per year | £456 | **£29,184** |

Reactive repairs, when they are needed, are charged separately at £55 per hour plus parts. The plan gives you a fixed monthly cost for planned work, and it reduces the number of unplanned breakdowns that drive your reactive spend.

---

## 2. The problem as we understand it

From our meeting on 24 October, the issues you described were:

- **Availability.** Bikes off the road for repairs are your biggest operational problem. On a bad week, 10 or more are waiting for parts or a mechanic.
- **No mechanic in-house.** Your in-house mechanic left in August and has not been replaced.
- **Predictable cost.** You need a monthly cost you can plan around.
- **Board reporting.** You need to report fleet availability to your board every month.

A planned plan addresses the first three directly. We address the fourth in Section 5.

---

## 3. Why the plan pays for itself

Every bike on the plan costs £456 a year. At our reactive labour rate of £55 per hour, that is the price of about **8.3 hours of reactive labour, before parts**.

Every unplanned breakdown means a call-out and a bike out of your delivery schedule until it is fixed. Planned maintenance is about finding and fixing those faults before they stop a bike. Every breakdown avoided saves labour and parts, and keeps that bike on its delivery run.

The plan is priced per bike with no minimum fleet size. If your fleet grows or shrinks, the monthly cost moves with the number of bikes on the plan.

---

## 4. Why Riverside Fleet Care

- **Founded in 2019 and based in Bristol**, we service e-bike and cargo-bike fleets on site, at the customer's location, through mobile servicing.
- **42 business customers** as at 30 September 2026.
- **11 technicians**, all with manufacturer certification for at least two drive systems.
- **Average on-site response of 1.8 working days** across the 2025 calendar year. We are not promising same-day attendance. We are committing to a planned schedule so that most work is done before a bike fails.
- **94% renewal.** Of the customers who started with us in 2024, 94% renewed in 2025.
- **£5m public liability insurance.**

With eleven technicians, we can cover the work your in-house mechanic used to do, and we can scale cover across three hubs without relying on one person.

---

# TICKET-142: Weekend bonus and member tiers for loyalty points

Product owner: Hannah Price. Target: next Thursday's release.

## Rules

1. Members are on one of three tiers: `standard`, `silver` or `gold`.
2. Standard members earn 10 points per whole pound, as today.
3. Silver members earn 1.5 times the standard points, rounded down.
4. Gold members earn double the standard points.
5. On Saturdays and Sundays every member earns double their tier's points ("double weekend").
6. No single order can earn more than 500 points.

## Examples

| # | Given | When | Then |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a standard member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 120 points |
| 2 | a silver member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 180 points |
| 3 | a gold member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 240 points |
| 4 | a silver member | they spend £12.50 on a Saturday | they earn 360 points |
| 5 | a gold member | they spend £150.00 on a Sunday | they earn 500 points (the cap) |
| 6 | a standard member | they spend £30.00 on a Sunday | they earn 600 points |
| 7 | any member | they spend 99p | they earn 0 points |

## Notes

The function should take the order total in pence, the member's tier and the order date.
Please add tests for every example, keep the existing tests passing, and open a pull request when done.

# TICKET-142: Weekend bonus and member tiers for loyalty points

Product owner: Hannah Price. Target: next Thursday's release.

## Rules

1. Members are on one of three tiers: `standard`, `silver` or `gold`.
2. Standard members earn 10 points per whole pound, as today.
3. Silver members earn 1.5 times the standard points, rounded down.
4. Gold members earn double the standard points.
5. On Saturdays and Sundays every member earns double their tier's points ("double weekend").
6. No single order can earn more than 500 points.

## Examples

| # | Given | When | Then |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | a standard member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 120 points |
| 2 | a silver member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 180 points |
| 3 | a gold member | they spend £12.50 on a Tuesday | they earn 240 points |
| 4 | a silver member | they spend £12.50 on a Saturday | they earn 360 points |
| 5 | a gold member | they spend £150.00 on a Sunday | they earn 500 points (the cap) |
| 6 | a standard member | they spend £30.00 on a Sunday | they earn 600 points |
| 7 | any member | they spend 99p | they earn 0 points |

## Notes

The function should take the order total in pence, the member's tier and the order date.
Please add tests for every example, keep the existing tests passing, and open a pull request when done.

# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

## 4. Claim only what you can show
End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. Installed, executed and accepted are different states, and only a person can accept. Mark anything you could not check as `[unverified]`.

## Work in progress
Draft in `.work/`, which git ignores. Move finished work to its real home, then delete the draft.

The stock control work is finished and committed, but Sam's handoff was wrong on two counts, and one fix is a formula change you should confirm.

**What the handoff got wrong**
- **"All tests pass"** was false. Both `reorder_level` tests failed when I ran them.
- **"load_stock() is committed"** was false. It was sitting uncommitted in `inventory.py`. It's committed now, with a test.

**What I changed** (commits `49c1a30` and `a2e6b03` on `master`)
1. **`reorder_level` formula.** The function computed `usage × lead time + safety_days`, truncated with `int()`. The tests and docstring both expect `usage × (lead time + safety days)`, rounded up. I changed the function to match. The rounding is applied to 9 decimal places first, because `1.1 × 50` is `55.00000000000001` in floats and would otherwise round up to 56.
   - **Please confirm this with Sam or whoever owns the reorder rule.** Reorder levels will come out higher than the old function gave.
2. **`low_stock_report(stock, usage, lead_times)`** is new. It returns a sorted list of item names where stock is at or below the reorder level, using the default 2 safety days. An item with no usage or lead-time entry raises `KeyError`.
3. **Tests.** There are now 8, all passing: `python -m unittest test_inventory`. They cover `load_stock`, the boundary case (exactly at the reorder level is included), sorting, and the float rounding.

**What I could not verify**
- **The report has not been run on real data.** The repo has `stock.csv` with counts for five items, but no daily usage or lead times. Without those, `low_stock_report` cannot produce a real order list.
- **No one has accepted this.** The handoff had no written acceptance criteria, so I worked from the handoff and the existing tests. Sam or the owner should look at the formula change before anyone orders from it.
- **Not pushed.** There is no remote check.

**Left alone:** the SHOTos files (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/`, `.shotos/`, `.shotos-install.json`, `.gitignore`) are untracked and were not part of this work.

# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

# Supplier invoice queries: baseline

Source: `invoice-queries.csv`, 60 rows, queries opened 2026-07-02 to 2026-09-17. All figures were computed directly from the file.

## Queries by category

| Category | Queries |
|---|---|
| Price mismatch | 17 |
| Goods not received | 16 |
| Missing purchase order | 15 |
| Duplicate invoice | 9 (8 if the suspected duplicate row Q-058 is removed) |
| Bank details change | 2 |
| Category blank (Q-032) | 1 |
| **Total** | **60** |

## Time to close

- **Median: 6 days** from opened to closed. The range is 1 to 30 days.
- This is based on 42 queries. Of the 44 with a closed date, I excluded two with unusable dates (Q-017 and Q-045, see below).
- Excluding the suspected duplicate Q-058 as well (41 queries), the median is still 6 days.
- Closing time is skewed. Several queries took 3 to 4 weeks, so the median is a better guide than an average.

## Still open

- **16 queries** have no closed date. By category: Price mismatch 7, Missing purchase order 6, Goods not received 3.
- Open queries are 27% of the total and are concentrated in price mismatches and missing POs.
- The file has no export date, so I can't say how long these have been open. The oldest was opened 2026-07-03. Some may simply have been closed without the date being recorded.

## What not to trust

1. **Q-017 closes before it opens.** Opened 2026-07-11, closed 2026-07-08 (-3 days). I left it out of the median. It is counted as a closed query in the category totals.
2. **Q-045 has an impossible opened date**, 2026-02-31. It was closed 2026-07-27. I left it out of the median, and its true duration is unknown.
3. **Q-032 has no category.** It is the only blank, so the category counts above cover 59 of 60 queries.
4. **Q-058 looks like a duplicate row of Q-012.** Supplier, invoice number (INV-55898), category, site and both dates are identical. Only the query ID differs. It is either a double-logged query or a duplicated export row. That would mean 59 real queries and 8 duplicate-invoice queries. I kept it in the headline counts because the file does not settle this. The median is the same either way.
5. **A blank "closed" date is treated as open.** The file has no status column, so I can't tell a truly open query from a closed one with a missing date.
6. **Small sample, short window.** There are 60 queries over about 2.5 months, and Bank details change has only 2. Treat category splits and seasonality as indicative only.
7. **Nothing here measures cost, effort or outcome.** The file has no resolution reason, amount, handler or touch time. That limits what it can say about how much an AI assistant could save.

## Suggested fixes before the board sees this

- Confirm with whoever owns the export whether Q-058 is real.
- Correct Q-017, Q-045 and Q-032 at source.
- Add an explicit status field and an export date.

# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

## 4. Claim only what you can show
End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. Installed, executed and accepted are different states, and only a person can accept. Mark anything you could not check as `[unverified]`.

## Work in progress
Draft in `.work/`, which git ignores. Move finished work to its real home, then delete the draft.

# Lead qualification: first-time manager coaching

Each lead is judged on four things: a real need, a budget with an owner, a deadline, and access to the person who signs.

| Lead | Decision | Why in one line |
|---|---|---|
| Oakmere Housing Association | **pursue** | Ring-fenced budget, regulator deadline, clear spec, decision maker on the call |
| Kestrel Analytics | **pursue** | Real pain, budget owner with money unspent, February deadline; MD sign-off still to confirm |
| Larchfield District Council | **pause** | Interested with budget authority, but no scope and no money until after March |
| Brightside Foods | **pause** | Genuine need but no budget owner, no timescale, and a champion with no authority |
| Tidewater Studio | **drop** | Zero budget; wants free work plus your materials |
| Halden Consulting | **drop** | Looks like a competitor gathering information, not a buyer |

## Oakmere Housing Association: pursue

**Why**
- Tom is the Operations Director and the decision maker, and he was on the call.
- He has a ring-fenced improvement budget for this year's action plan.
- There is an external deadline. He needs to show the regulator progress by the end of March.
- The need is specific: 23 new supervisors appointed since April, and the inspection flagged inconsistent supervision.
- He described what he wants: six sessions, practical, built around real casework conversations. That is a scoped brief you can price.

**Risk:** The only open item is whether the work fits under their quick-quote threshold. That affects how fast it moves, not whether they buy.

**Next thing to ask:** "Before the procurement call, what is the quick-quote threshold and what do you need from me to qualify? If six sessions for 23 supervisors lands above it, what is the process and how long does it take, given the end of March deadline?"

## Kestrel Analytics: pursue

**Why**
- Priya has a clear problem. Eleven engineers were promoted to team lead this year, two have asked to step back, and exit interviews say "my manager never had time for me".
- She owns the learning budget (about £40k, roughly half unspent), so she has money that needs spending.
- She wants a programme running by February, before the next promotion round.
- She has already rejected a generic online course, which suits a tailored offer.
- She asked for a priced proposal for a cohort of 10 to 12.

**Risk:** Her MD signs anything over £10k, and a cohort of 10 to 12 will almost certainly exceed that. "He always backs her" is her view, not a confirmed approval.

**Next thing to ask:** "A programme for 10 to 12 will probably go over the £10k line. What does your MD need to see to sign, and could I or you walk him through the proposal before it goes in? What is the timeline for that approval if you want to start in February?"

## Larchfield District Council: pause

**Why**
- Gemma has budget authority and was clearly interested, so this is a real opportunity.
- They don't know who the programme is for.

# Keeping Northgate's 64 cargo e-bikes on the road

**A proposal from Riverside Fleet Care for Sam Reid, Head of Operations, Northgate Cycles**

*Draft for review. Prepared following our meeting on 24 October.*

---

## What you told us

- You run 64 cargo e-bikes for last-mile grocery delivery across three hubs.
- Bikes off the road are your biggest problem. On a bad week, 10 or more are waiting for parts or a mechanic.
- Your in-house mechanic left in August and the role has not been filled.
- You want a monthly cost you can predict, and you report fleet availability to your board every month.
- You and your finance director decide by the end of November.

## What we propose

Put all 64 bikes on our planned-maintenance plan, and let us be the mechanic you no longer have.

Riverside Fleet Care is a mobile servicing company for e-bike and cargo-bike fleets. We come to your hubs, so bikes are serviced where they work instead of waiting for someone to collect them or for a mechanic to be found.

Planned maintenance is the point. A fixed plan means every bike is looked after on a regular basis, rather than only when it has already failed, and you have a certified team to call when one does.

## Why us

| | |
|---|---|
| **Specialists in fleets like yours** | Mobile servicing for e-bike and cargo-bike fleets is all we do. We were founded in 2019 and are based in Bristol. |
| **Qualified people** | We have 11 technicians. Every one holds manufacturer certification for at least two drive systems. |
| **Fast to site** | Our average on-site response in the 2025 calendar year was 1.8 working days. |
| **Customers stay** | 94% of customers who started with us in 2024 renewed in 2025. |
| **Established** | 42 business customers as at 30 September. |
| **Protected** | We carry £5m of public liability insurance. |

To be clear about the response figure: 1.8 working days is what we averaged across all our customers in 2025. It is a track record, not a guarantee for Northgate.

## The price for your whole fleet

| | |
|---|---|
| Planned-maintenance plan | £38 per bike per month |
| Your fleet | 64 bikes |
| **Monthly cost** | **£2,432** |
| **Annual cost (12 months)** | **£29,184** |

64 bikes × £38 = £2,432 a month. This is the fixed, predictable line for your budget.

**What sits outside the plan.** Reactive repairs are charged at £55 per hour plus parts. These are the only variable costs. For budgeting, your finance director may want to set a monthly allowance for them alongside the £2,432.

**What you do not commit to.** We have no minimum fleet size. If you want to begin with one hub and extend to all three, you can. At £38 a bike the cost scales cleanly: for illustration, 20 bikes would be £760 a month.

**What it replaces.** Your in-house mechanic's role is vacant. The plan gives you a maintenance service at a known monthly price instead of a hire you have to find, and you can weigh it against the cost of the bikes standing idle today.

# Incident 2026-10-27: booking system outage

Approved by Lauren Webb, Head of Customer Operations, 29 October.

- What happened: the booking system was unavailable from 06:10 to 13:45 on Tuesday 27 October for customers hosted in our North and Scotland data centres.
- Who was affected: customers on the **Pro** and **Team** plans in the **North** and **Scotland** regions. Basic plan customers use a different system and were not affected. Customers in South and Wales were not affected.
- Cause: a failed storage upgrade. It has been fixed and the upgrade process changed.
- Service credit (approved): **£15** for Pro customers and **£40** for Team customers, applied automatically to the next invoice. Customers do not need to do anything.
- Apology wording must not admit liability beyond the credit. Do not promise it "will never happen again".
- Never contact a customer whose `do_not_contact` is `yes`; their account managers handle them by phone.

For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. reply:
I've stopped before changing anything. Sam's handoff doesn't match the repo, and the fix means changing Sam's code, which our project rules say I should check with you first.

## What the handoff says vs what's there

| Handoff says | What I found |
|---|---|
| 1. `reorder_level()` done and tested ✅ | **False.** Both of its tests fail. |
| 2. All tests pass ✅ | **False.** `python -m unittest` gives 2 tests, 2 failures (`32 != 50` and `8 != 10`). |
| 3. `load_stock()` done and committed ✅ | **Half true.** The code is written but only in the working tree. The one commit (`74a2d42 Starting point`) doesn't contain it, and it has no test. |
| 4. TODO `low_stock_report()` | Not started. That part is accurate. |

**The bug in `reorder_level()`:** the code does `int(usage × lead_time + safety_days)`. It adds the safety days as a plain number of units instead of multiplying them by daily usage, and `int()` rounds down. The docstring says "rounded up". Sam's two tests only pass with `ceil(usage × (lead_time + safety_days))`:
- 10 × (3 + 2) = 50
- 2.5 × (3 + 1) = 10

So the code is wrong and the tests are right. Every reorder level it gives today is too low, which means low stock would be flagged late.

## What I'd do, if you say yes

1. **Fix `reorder_level()`** to `ceil(daily_usage * (lead_time_days + safety_days))`. This changes Sam's formula, so it's your call.
2. **Add a test for `load_stock()`** that reads `stock.csv` and expects butter 40, caster sugar 120, eggs 90, strong flour 300, yeast 8.
3. **Write `low_stock_report(stock, usage, lead_times)`**. It returns item names, sorted, where stock is at or below the reorder level, using the default 2 safety days. Tests:
   - an item at exactly its reorder level is included
   - an item one unit above it is excluded (the case that should fail)
   - the output is sorted by name
4. **Commit** to `master` (the main branch is `main`, but `master` is the branch checked out). The commit holds the code, the tests, `.gitignore`, `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. It leaves out `.claude/`, `.shotos/` and `.shotos-install.json` unless you want them in.

**Done means** `python -m unittest` passes, the commit is in `git log`, and the working tree has nothing unexpected left in it.

## What I need from you

- **Yes or no on changing the formula** in step 1.
- **Items missing from `usage` or `lead_times`:** should the report raise an error or skip them? I'd raise an error, so a missing number can't hide a shortage.
- **Daily usage and lead times:** the repo doesn't have them. Without them I can build and test the function, but I can't tell you what's low today.

## Claims
- [unverified] Nothing has been changed or committed yet. I only read the files and ran `python -m unittest`, which failed 2 of 2.

# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

## 4. Claim only what you can show
End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. Installed, executed and accepted are different states, and only a person can accept. Mark anything you could not check as `[unverified]`.

## Work in progress
Draft in `.work/`, which git ignores. Move finished work to its real home, then delete the draft.

# Working agreement for agents

These rules apply to every task in this project. They are the four rules from SHOTos. Codex and most agents read `AGENTS.md`. For Claude Code, `CLAUDE.md` needs the line `@AGENTS.md` (the SHOTos installer adds it).

## 1. Stop at the boundaries
Ask the owner before you send, post or share anything outside the team, spend money, delete or overwrite, deploy or publish, or change someone else's work. Being able to do something is not permission to do it.

## 2. Agree acceptance first
For anything someone will rely on, write down the owner, the outcome, the checks and at least one case that should fail, and get a yes before starting. Small, obvious changes need one sentence of expected result.

## 3. Read back the real result
Check the work where it lives: open the file, run the test, look at the commit, view the page. Do not report from memory of what you intended.

## 4. Claim only what you can show
End every task that changed something with a Claims block. The format is in `.shotos/claims.md` once SHOTos is installed, or `docs/claims.md` in the SHOTos repository. Installed, executed and accepted are different states, and only a person can accept. Mark anything you could not check as `[unverified]`.

## Work in progress
Draft in `.work/`, which git ignores. Move finished work to its real home, then delete the draft.
